knownFor.label: Coffee economy
knownFor.note: Brazil became the world’s largest coffee producer.

knownFor.label: Pedro II
knownFor.note: A long-reigning emperor interested in science.

location.value: Modern Brazil (and Uruguay until 1828), with its capital at Rio de Janeiro.

terrain.value: The Amazon basin, the Atlantic coast, highlands, and the Pampas in the south.

resources.value: Coffee (42% of exports by the 1840s), sugar, rubber, cotton and gold.

disasters.value: The Great Drought in the Northeast (1877–78) caused a severe famine.
disasters.source: Barman, Citizen Emperor: Pedro II and the Making of Brazil (1999)

urbanisation.value: Rio de Janeiro was the capital and largest city. Mostly rural plantations.

disease.value: Yellow fever and cholera epidemics in the 19th century.
disease.source: Barman, Citizen Emperor: Pedro II and the Making of Brazil (1999)

migration.value: Enslaved Africans were brought by force until the trade was effectively ended (1850). European immigration grew later. In 1872 the population was 38.3% pardo, 38.1% white, 19.7% black and 3.9% Indigenous.

economicBase.value: Plantation exports (coffee, sugar) worked by enslaved people.

tradeRoutes.value: Coffee exports to Europe and the US. Railways from 1854 (9,200 km by 1889).

wealth.value: In 1850 its exports were the highest in Latin America. No GDP figure is given in the sources checked.

moneyAndTax.value: The real (currency). Revenue mainly from trade duties.

inequality.value: Extreme inequality based on slavery and large estates.

governmentType.value: A unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy (Constitution of 1824), with a “moderating power” held by the emperor.

keyRulers.value: Pedro I (1822–1831). The regency (1831–1840). Pedro II (1831–1889, came of age 1840). Princess Isabel (regent, signed the abolition of slavery).

succession.value: Hereditary in the Braganza dynasty. Isabel, the heir, was not widely accepted as a future female monarch.

institutions.value: The 1824 Constitution, the General Assembly (Senate and Chamber of Deputies), and parliamentary cabinets.

stability.value: Provincial revolts in the 1830s–40s (the Ragamuffin War, Cabanagem, Balaiada, the Praieira revolt). Stability under Pedro II.

eliteConflict.value: Conflict between liberals and conservatives, and army discontent in the 1880s, which led to the 1889 coup.

armyAndTech.value: An army and navy that grew strong during the Paraguayan War.

majorWars.value: The War of Independence (1822–24). The Cisplatine War (lost Uruguay, 1828). The Platine War (1851–52). The Paraguayan War (1864–70).

territoryChange.value: About 8.3 million km² in 1889 (Wikipedia infobox). Lost Cisplatina (Uruguay) in 1828.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Argentina and Paraguay. Allied with Argentina and Uruguay against Paraguay.

inventions.value: Railways (1854), telegraph (1852, transatlantic link 1874), and public electric lighting (1883).

scienceEducation.value: Pedro II was a keen patron of science and education. Literacy remained low.
scienceEducation.source: Barman, Citizen Emperor: Pedro II and the Making of Brazil (1999)

openness.value: Open to European ideas, immigrants and technology.
openness.source: Barman, Citizen Emperor: Pedro II and the Making of Brazil (1999)

religion.value: Roman Catholicism was the state religion. Afro-Brazilian religions were practised among the enslaved and their descendants.

artsArchitecture.value: Romantic literature (Machado de Assis began his career). Neoclassical architecture in Rio.
artsArchitecture.source: Barman, Citizen Emperor: Pedro II and the Making of Brazil (1999)

socialStructure.value: Landowners and merchants, free people of colour, the enslaved (abolished 1888), and Indigenous peoples.

sharedIdentity.value: A Brazilian national identity built around the monarchy. Motto: “Independence or Death!”

neighbours.value: Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia, Peru and the European colonies of the Guianas.

ideasReligions.value: Liberal and abolitionist ideas from Europe. Positivist ideas influenced the republicans.
ideasReligions.source: Barman, Citizen Emperor: Pedro II and the Making of Brazil (1999)

colonisation.value: A former Portuguese colony (independent 1822). Its economy depended on slavery, the last in the Americas to be abolished (1888).

riseSignals.value: Peaceful separation from Portugal under a member of its royal family (1822), and a coffee boom.

peakPeriod.value: The mid-reign of Pedro II (1850s–1870s), with stability, growth and victory in the Paraguayan War.

declineSignals.value: Abolition (1888) angered planters. Army discontent, republican ideas, and doubts about Isabel’s succession.

outcome.value: A military coup on 15 November 1889 overthrew the monarchy and created the First Brazilian Republic. The imperial family went into exile.

sources.value: Censuses (1872), government records and correspondence. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Barman (1999).

overallCertainty.value: High for events and population (1872 census). Historians debate whether 1889 was a coup or a revolution.

sources: Wikipedia: Empire of Brazil (infobox, checked 6 Nov 2026)
